ledger.note: April 1356: Zhu Yuanzhang takes Jiqing and renames it Yingtian. In April, Zhu entered Jiqing (present-day Nanjing), which he renamed Yingtian; the Red Turban page dates it 10 April; in May Han Lin'er named him head of Jiangnan Province.

region.text: southwestern Jiangsu and Anhui south of the Yangtze

ledger.note: By the start of 1360 (bridging): southwestern Jiangsu and Anhui south of the Yangtze. At the start of the year, Zhu controlled southwestern Jiangsu, all of Anhui south of the Yangtze, and inland Zhejiang. The page gives the holding, not the dates of the conquests (it has 1355-1357 attacks toward Suzhou), so the gain is placed in 1359.
1361: Han Lin'er appoints Zhu Duke of Wu (Wu Guogong). Han Lin'er appointed Zhu Duke of Wu, the origin of the state's name.

region.text: the middle Yangtze and Lake Poyang between Anqing, Jiujiang and Nanchang

ledger.note: 1361: Zhu takes Jiujiang from the Han, the Han retake it, and Zhu's fleet takes it again in September. Zhu had captured Jiujiang earlier that year; September 1361: Zhu's fleet defeated the Han fleet, captured Jiujiang, and failed to take Hanyang.

region.text: Jiujiang and Anqing on the Yangtze

ledger.note: 1361 (before August): Zhu captures Jiujiang from the Han. Chen Han page: "Zhu Yuanzhang successfully captured Jiujiang and blocked the remaining forces of Chen Youliang in Wuchang." The page does not say Zhu captured Anqing before August, but it says the Han were "retaking Jiujiang and Anqing in August 1361", which implies Zhu held both; Anqing is that reading, hence confidence 2. Mirrors chen-han /ledger/4.

region.text: Jiujiang and Anqing on the Yangtze

ledger.note: August 1361: the Han counter-offensive retakes Jiujiang and Anqing. Chen Han page: the Han government "launched a counter-offensive, successfully retaking Jiujiang and Anqing in August 1361." Mirrors chen-han /ledger/5, which maps only Jiujiang.

region.text: Jiujiang

ledger.note: September 1361: Zhu's fleet defeats the Han fleet and takes Jiujiang; it fails to take Hanyang.

region.text: Jiangxi

ledger.note: Early 1362: Nanchang surrenders and Zhu holds Jiangxi. Han garrison commander Hu Mei surrendered Nanchang to Zhu, giving Zhu control of Jiangxi.

region.text: Anfeng (Shouxian) in Anhui, the Song court's seat 1359-1363; no page opened says who held it after Zhu's army arrived in March 1363

ledger.note: March 1363 (bridging): Zhu's army relieves Anfeng. Liu Futong page: "Zhu Yuanzhang and his general, Xu Da, rescued Han Lin'er in March" after Zhang Shicheng's general Lu Zhen took Anfeng in February. No page opened says who held Anfeng afterwards (Liu Futong, Han Lin'er, Hongwu Emperor, Red Turban and Wu pages are silent), so the transfer to Zhu is the dossier's reading. Mirrors zhang-shicheng-s-wu /ledger.

region.text: Chuzhou, the court seat of Han Lin'er's Song from 1363 (han-song)

ledger.note: June 1363 or later (bridging): Han Lin'er's court is housed at Chuzhou. Han Lin'er page: "Han and his court were then relocated to Chuzhou"; the page gives no month for the move (it follows Chen Youliang's attack on Zhu in June 1363) and does not say who controlled Chuzhou. The Red Turban page says Zhu had gained Chuzhou in 1353. Recorded only to mirror han-song /ledger (gain of the 40 km court-seat circle, June 1363); it is a map bookkeeping entry, not a recorded loss of Zhu's control.

region.text: the frontier of Zhu's Jiangnan with Zhang's Wu

ledger.note: 1364: the war with Zhang Shicheng's Wu begins. Early 1364: Zhu Yuanzhang also declared himself King of Wu, starting a war between the two states; Zhang's preemptive attack came in late 1364 and was repelled in spring 1365.
4 February 1364: Zhu proclaims himself King of Wu (Wu wang). On 4 February, Zhu proclaimed himself King of Wu. The page does not say 'Prince'.

region.text: Wuchang

ledger.note: March 1364: Chen Li surrenders Wuchang and Zhu begins to absorb the Han lands. March 1364 (Wuchang): As Zhu's army approached Wuchang again, Chen Li surrendered, ending the state.

region.text: the middle Yangtze and Lake Poyang between Anqing, Jiujiang and Nanchang

ledger.note: March 1364: the fighting with the Han ends at Wuchang. Between 1361 and 1364 fell the Battle of Lake Poyang (30 August to 3 October 1363, Chen Youliang killed by an arrow); Chen Li surrendered in March 1364.

ledger.note: April 1365: the Han lands of Hubei and Hunan are absorbed. Until April 1365, Zhu occupied and absorbed the Han territories in Hubei, Hunan, and Jiangxi; Xu Da pacified Huguang (Hongwu Emperor page).

ledger.note: 23 January 1368: Zhu Yuanzhang proclaims the Ming at Yingtian. Zhu proclaimed himself emperor, named the dynasty Da Ming, and designated 1368 the first Hongwu year (Hongwu Emperor page); the Ming page's infobox: 'Established in Nanjing: 23 January 1368'; the Red Turban page says 12 January. The same state continues as the Ming.

notes:
Written for ea-06-x from the Hongwu Emperor page, with the Chen Han, Zhang Shicheng, Wu (Zhang Shicheng), Fang Guozhen, Ming dynasty and Red Turban Rebellions pages. Wikipedia has no article for this state (the Chen Han and Wu infoboxes name Zhu Yuanzhang's state of Wu in plain text), so the Hongwu Emperor page is the source of identity, titles and shapes. Treatment: the Wu continues without a break into the Ming (same state, same ruler, one proclamation on 23 January 1368); the dossier ends there and names ming-dynasty as successor, but the colour agent and the Ming group should treat the two as one state with a rename if the Ming dossier starts in 1368 (Cliopatria's Ming row starts in 1375). Vassalage: from May 1356 to January 1367 Zhu was nominally subordinate to Han Lin'er's Song; that is recorded in han-song as a vassal_start/vassal_end with counterpart zhu-yuanzhang-s-wu. Disagreements: the Ming proclamation is 12 January (Red Turban page) or 23 January 1368 (Hongwu Emperor page and the Ming infobox); the Red Turban page calls Zhu 'Prince of Wu', the Hongwu page King of Wu; the Hongwu page, in the summariser's reading, says Zhu occupied southern Jiangxi in 1355-1357, which conflicts with the Chen Han page's Jiangxi surrender of 1362 and is not used. Not on any page: the dates of the conquests of Wannan, southwestern Jiangsu and inland Zhejiang (1356-1359), the names of the four inland Zhejiang prefectures, the cities of the 1366 northern campaign, and areas for the keyframes. The 1359 and 1366 northern gains are confidence 1. Counterparts needing dossiers: yuan-dynasty (ea-06-a), ming-dynasty (the Ming group), and the other six states of this batch.

Revision of 2026-10-24 after the adversarial review (fail: overlapping shapes). (1) The Nanjing circle no longer crosses the Yangtze: Zhu's circle is {minus: [Nanjing 100 km, the Gaoyou-Taizhou-Xinghua district]}, in every keyframe, in /ledger/0, /ledger/20 and the successors, so the shape no longer overlaps zhang-shicheng-s-wu (it shared 89-100 cells each year 1356-1365). (2) The 1361 Jiujiang gain and August loss now mirror chen-han /ledger/4-5; Anqing is mapped on both because the Chen Han page says the Han were 'retaking' it, although no page says how Zhu got it. (3) Anfeng: a conf-1 gain in March 1363 mirrors zhang-shicheng-s-wu; all pages opened are silent on who held Anfeng afterwards. (4) The Chuzhou court-seat circle of han-song is out of Zhu's shape from 1363 to January 1367 (conf-1 loss and conf-2 gain back); the Red Turban page says Zhu had gained Chuzhou in 1353, so this is bookkeeping. (5) The 1364 keyframe now holds the Wuchang circle only and Huguang starts in a 1365 keyframe, as in the ledger (Chen Han page: occupation until April 1365).
